hints: Look closely at what Km actually measures on a rate graph, the substrate concentration needed to reach half of Vmax.
Ask yourself, if an enzyme holds its substrate very tightly (high affinity), will it need a lot or a little substrate to get to half speed?
walkthrough:
**Recall what Km really means**

Think of Km as a helpful number, not a scary formula. It is the substrate concentration that gives half the maximum rate.

Key definition:
$$K_m = \text{[substrate] when rate} = \frac{V_{max}}{2}$$

**Check statement 1 about affinity and Km**

High affinity means the enzyme grabs substrate easily, even when there is very little around. So you need only a low substrate concentration to reach half speed. That means high affinity gives low Km. Statement 1 is correct.

**Check statement 2 about speed and statement 3 about half occupancy**

If affinity is low, the enzyme struggles to form enzyme-substrate complexes, so fewer reactions happen per second and the rate is slower. Statement 2 is correct.

At Km the rate is half of Vmax because about half the active sites are filled at any moment. Statement 3 is correct. So 1, 2 and 3 are all correct.

options.A: Correct and reassuring. Statements 1, 2 and 3 all match the definition of Km as the substrate concentration for half Vmax and its inverse link to affinity.
options.B: Close but incomplete. It correctly includes 1 and 2 but wrongly leaves out 3, which is the textbook definition of Km.
options.C: Close but incomplete. It correctly includes 1 and 3 but wrongly leaves out 2, since low affinity does mean slower ES formation and slower rate.
options.D: Close but incomplete. It correctly includes 2 and 3 but wrongly leaves out 1, since high affinity definitely means low Km.
